claims.evidence: NHS About page: anti-sickness medicine, prescribed to prevent or treat nausea and vomiting, including with migraine; prescription-only.
MHRA/EMA review: restricted dose and duration because of neurological risk; NHS safety alert says short-term use (up to 5 days). NHS: usually only for a short time.
NHS About page: used to help stop you feeling or being sick.
NHS: also prescribed to treat the sickness that can happen during a migraine.
MHRA update: in children 1-18 only second-line for prevention of delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea/vomiting and treatment of established postoperative nausea/vomiting.

No UK source retrieved says metoclopramide is a dopamine blocker (only vet label/patent via non-UK sources). Formularies list it with domperidone; MHRA calls domperidone 'a dopamine antagonist with antiemetic properties'.
claims.newSentence: NHS formularies list metoclopramide together with domperidone, which the MHRA describes as a dopamine antagonist with anti-sickness properties.

claims.evidence: Accurate: none of the NHS/MHRA pages retrieved describe a mechanism for metoclopramide.
NHS About/Side effects pages: drowsiness and diarrhoea are the most common side effects.
NHS side effects page lists low mood/depression among common effects, but tics and tremors are listed under the serious uncontrollable-movement effect, not as common.
claims.newSentence: The NHS also lists low mood or depression among the common side effects.

claims.evidence: Maxolon 10mg tablet leaflet/SmPC: disturbances in vision possible; drowsiness, dizziness, dyskinesia and dystonia may affect vision and ability to drive/operate machinery. NHS says not to drive if it makes you sleepy or affects vision. Author's URL (oral solution PIL) not the page seen.
claims.newSentence: Leaflets say it may affect vision and the ability to drive or use machines.

claims.evidence: NHS side effects: most common serious side effect is uncontrollable movements such as tics, tremors, muscle stiffness and spasms.
MHRA: risk of acute neurological effects is higher in children than in adults.
Generic site signposting; NHS page says call a doctor or 111 for unusual movements. Contains no dose/cut-off. Keep.
NHS Who can page: most adults and children aged 1 year and over can take it.
NHS Who can page: epilepsy/fits, Parkinson's disease, previous allergic reaction listed as reasons it may not suit.

Highland formulary: contraindicated in GI obstruction, perforation or haemorrhage; MHRA DHPC/SmPC and Derby/Somerset formularies: contraindicated under 1 year. Text seen from Highland formulary, not Dorset.
NHS other-medicines page: can interact with levodopa, sleep-inducing medicines such as diazepam or amitriptyline, and other anti-sickness medicines; tell a doctor or pharmacist.
NHS: not enough evidence to say herbal remedies/supplements are safe with it; some can worsen side effects.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says some herbal remedies and supplements can make the side effects of metoclopramide worse.

claims.evidence: NHS main page: best not to drink alcohol as it increases risk of side effects; common-questions page is stricter.
NHS: usually only for a short time (up to 5 days) because of side-effect risk.
MHRA excerpt says short-term use only; no retrieved text says a prescriber reviews the need.
claims.newSentence: The MHRA limits its use to short-term treatment.
